questions.q: According to this lesson, what real gap remains even after a network is correctly segmented into web, app, and data tiers with NSGs?
options: NSGs cannot be applied to subnets, only to individual VMs
Workloads sitting next to each other inside the same tier can usually still reach one another freely, since the NSG only enforces the boundary between tiers
Hub-spoke topology is incompatible with NSGs
Tier-based segmentation eliminates the need for any firewall at all
questions.explain: Tier-level segmentation enforces the boundary between zones, but a shared NSG rule inside one tier (like the app tier) typically still lets every workload in that tier reach every other workload in it.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of micro-segmentation, as described in this lesson?
options: Policy is written against an individual workload rather than a subnet or IP range
It replaces NSGs and hub-spoke topology entirely and makes them unnecessary
It only applies to north-south traffic crossing the perimeter
It requires every workload to use the exact same IP address permanently
questions.explain: Micro-segmentation shrinks the unit that enforcement policy targets from a subnet-level IP range down to a single workload, such as one service or container.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that IP-based policy rules break down in dynamic, autoscaled environments?
options: IP-based rules are always slower to evaluate than identity-based rules
Firewalls cannot parse IPv6 addresses
Containers and autoscaled instances get rescheduled with new IPs constantly, so an address range stops reliably describing what is actually running there
IP addresses are considered personally identifiable information under most compliance frameworks
questions.explain: In a dynamic environment, workloads move between hosts and get new IPs regularly, so a rule tied to an address range quickly stops matching what's actually deployed.

questions.q: What does a workload identity (such as a certificate or a signed label like app=payments-api) let a micro-segmentation policy do that an IP-based rule cannot?
options: Encrypt data at rest automatically
Eliminate the need for authentication entirely
Automatically generate compliance reports for auditors
Travel with the workload wherever it's rescheduled, since the policy is attached to what the workload is, not to its current address
questions.explain: Because the identity is attached to the workload itself rather than to a network location, the policy keeps applying correctly even after the workload moves to a new host or IP.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect micro-segmentation back to the NIST Zero Trust tenets covered in Chapter 1?
options: It applies the "dynamic, strictly enforced access decision" tenet to east-west, workload-to-workload traffic, not just user-to-resource access
It argues the NIST tenets apply only to user authentication and have no bearing on network traffic
It treats micro-segmentation as a replacement for the NIST tenets rather than an application of them
It claims NIST SP 800-207 does not address network segmentation at all
questions.explain: The lesson frames micro-segmentation as the same dynamic, strictly-enforced-access tenet from Chapter 1, now applied to workload-to-workload (east-west) traffic instead of only user access.
